To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the radiation dose to a stack of 10 layers of scintillating plastic is 1.3 x 10 to the minus 5th power rads/10 to the minus the 12th power protons/cm2.
the dose from neutral beam is about 1 mrad/10(12) protons, and the flux from neutral beam can be used for calibration of radiation damage in a calorimeter, but the radiation is highly nonuniform.
the radiation dose to a stack of lead and Bicron BC400 scintillator is 2.5 mR per 10^13 protons on target.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the radiation damage to scintillator caused by the neutral beam at the SSC.
radiation damage and radiation compensation.
the effects of radiation on scintillators and the use of radiation to measure the radiation environment in a high energy beam.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have demonstrated that radiation damage to scintillator can occur at the SSC.
the radiation environment of the stack is consistent with the predictions of the Monte Carlo code, FLUKA.
the radiation damage effects are not serious and can be easily compensated for by using a scintillator of sufficient thickness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the radiation effects in the scintillator are small and that the radiation effects can be easily compensated for in the electronics.
the fluxes are high enough for significant damage and compensation to be considered in the design of a calorimeter.

we have measured radiation damage and compensation in scintillators and lead, we have measured the dose from neutral beams, we have measured dose from charged beams, we have made a comparison of the radiation dose to scintillator from charged beams with that from neutral beams, and we have measured the effect of a magnetic field on radiation damage to scintillator
The main takeaway from our work is that

the radiation dose in a neutral beam can be determined by the use of radiochromic dye and that the dose is sufficient to cause significant damage in the scintillator, which can be compensated for by the use of wavelength shifters.
the radiation dose to scintillators in a stack is not proportional to the flux.
the radiation dose to a calorimeter is a complicated function of the calorimeter design, the beam conditions, and the location of the calorimeter.
